Faithfulness is better matched to the task, but only after the judge receives both research notes and the underlying search results.

A custom actionability judge asks whether reports provide concrete recommendations, risks, and forward-looking analysis. Voss builds its rubric from observed failures, separates instructions and data with XML tags, constrains output labels, and tests whether examples help. Small wording and formatting changes materially alter judgments. Human calibration exposes another problem: his own labels sometimes accept reports that violate his stated risk criterion. A golden dataset therefore needs consistent expert labeling, development/test separation, and attention to precision, recall, and borderline cases. Agreement on twelve development examples is encouraging, not strong evidence of production reliability.

Experiments compare the same inputs and evaluators before and after targeted prompt changes, with repeated runs to reveal variability. Explicit recommendations and instructions to return text improve actionability, but unsupported claims persist: faithfulness reaches only 3 of 48 improved-prompt runs. A subsequent model comparison improves faithfulness somewhat at four times the cost, while increased recommendation consistency largely comes from repeatedly choosing hold. Voss distinguishes succeeding at least once across several attempts from succeeding every time, an important difference for financial or support applications. The closing workflow integrates existing evaluators into Vitest and GitHub Actions, distinguishes release-blocking guardrails from aspirational targets, and recommends production sampling with alerts for sustained deterioration rather than isolated failures.
caveats: The supplied publisher transcript is untimed, and its provenance metadata does not establish semantic completeness.
The workshop uses a deliberately weak demonstration agent and a small dataset; its reported scores are not production benchmarks or evidence of investment quality.

The transcript contains questionable factual details, including describing Rivian as nonpublic, and inconsistent model-version references. These should not be treated as verified company facts or a reliable model catalog.
The demonstration does not solve the agent's faithfulness problem; production monitoring is recommended but not built during the session.
action_items: Instrument an existing agent and read roughly a dozen complete traces before deciding which failures to automate checks for.
Define quality with domain stakeholders, then implement separate checks for deterministic requirements, groundedness, and application-specific usefulness.
Build a small, carefully labeled golden dataset with development and held-out test splits; investigate judge disagreements instead of treating human labels as infallible.
Compare prompt or model changes on identical inputs across repeated runs, tracking cost and multiple quality dimensions rather than a single aggregate score.
Move stable checks into CI with explicit thresholds, then add difficult production cases to the dataset and monitor sustained score changes.

videos.title: An AI Agent Got Its User Banned From Resy — Keycard, JPMorgan Chase & AAuth
videos.overview: This panel examines why agent autonomy requires authorization tied to a specific mission, transaction, and changing environment—not just possession of credentials. Speakers from Keycard, JPMorgan Chase, and AAuth discuss resource budgets, independent enforcement, and tamper-resistant audit records, using an allegedly overzealous restaurant-booking agent as a concrete example.
key_points: Broad OAuth scopes and standing credentials often grant much more access than a particular agent instance needs for its current task.
A mission captures the human or organization's intended outcome and provides context for authorization decisions across multiple actions and potentially long-running workflows.
Runtime decisions should intersect organizational policy, task intent, user authority, prior actions, and environmental conditions rather than trust the worker agent's assertions alone.
AAuth's proposed budgets complement token expiration by limiting resource consumption and giving agents feedback about remaining capacity.
Keep enforcement and credentials outside the worker's sandbox, and separate supervision from execution so the agent cannot authorize its own actions.
Dynamic tool availability can reduce dangerous capability combinations, context clutter, wasted tokens, and ordinary task errors.
Audit records outside the agent's control should connect actions to the originating person, mission, and authorization context for investigation and accountability.
summary: Moderated by Allie Howe, the panel brings together Keycard CEO Ian, JPMorgan Chase security architect Michael Davis, and OAuth co-creator and AAuth founder Dick Hardt. They argue that enterprise autonomy is constrained less by model intelligence than by authorization systems built for humans and deterministic software. Coarse scopes cannot distinguish shopping assistance from production debugging, or one payment from a duplicate made seconds earlier. Davis compares safer adoption to onboarding a developer: begin with limited capabilities and expand them as confidence and contextual safeguards improve. Financial transaction authorization provides an analogy because it already considers a specific action at runtime rather than merely identifying an account holder.

Hardt describes an AAuth mission as an outcome assigned by a human or organization, with a mission identifier carried through subsequent actions for auditability. The mission may need clarification before execution, and it cannot override the person's existing authority. The panel advocates deterministic rules for prohibited actions and mandatory escalation, supplemented by contextual supervision where enumerating every policy would be impractical. Ian describes effective permissions as the intersection of business purpose and immediate task intent. Davis adds that context can change the answer: reading an executive's email is different when requested by an authorized administrative assistant. This approach is still nascent, not a capability the panel claims most enterprises already possess.

Agentic commerce makes the stakes tangible. According to the moderator, an Instinct agent seeking a Resy reservation made 200 API calls an hour and got its user's account banned. Hardt explains budgets that constrain both credential lifetime and resource consumption, with feedback allowing an agent to reason about scarcity and request additional allocation from supervision. The panel also discusses recognizable agent identity and interoperable protocols, arguing that website operators need ways to evaluate unfamiliar automated clients without relying solely on CAPTCHAs or closed vendor arrangements. Independent supervision would let users choose policy components separately from the agents performing work.

The proposed architecture places tools inside a controlled sandbox and authorization at an external egress boundary, keeping broad credentials away from the worker. Davis warns that poisoned memory and dangerous combinations of capabilities remain concerns; temporarily removing external tools during sensitive email work is one suggested mitigation. Authorization should also incorporate changing environmental signals, such as system vulnerabilities, location, and execution state. External audit logs preserve who requested what and why, supporting incident diagnosis and responsibility. The closing risk discussion is explicitly opinionated: Hardt emphasizes malicious actors and irresponsible deployments, Davis expresses confidence in engineering progress, and Ian considers existential catastrophe highly unlikely. None offers a measured probability or demonstrates that the proposed controls eliminate agent risk.
caveats: The supplied publisher transcript is untimed, and semantic completeness is not proven by its metadata.
The Resy, Pocket OS, and Hugging Face incidents are recounted by panelists without primary incident records in the supplied source.
The discussion presents emerging architecture and protocol proposals, not a reproducible implementation or quantitative comparison against existing authorization systems.
Claims about liability, the need for regulation, and catastrophic-risk probabilities are speakers' opinions rather than legal guidance or established risk estimates.
action_items: Give each agent task a mission identifier and record its requested outcome, responsible person or organization, and authorized boundaries.
Evaluate sensitive tool calls against task intent, organizational policy, recent actions, and environmental state rather than broad credential scopes alone.
Keep credentials, enforcement, and audit logs outside the worker agent's control; use an external boundary to mediate access.
Set explicit resource budgets with remaining-budget feedback and a supervised renewal path for agents that retry or consume paid services.
Review dangerous tool combinations and dynamically limit capabilities during sensitive workflows, reserving human escalation for meaningful exceptions.

videos.title: Teach Your Agent to Prove It's Done — Nick Nisi & Zack Proser, WorkOS
videos.overview: Nick Nisi and Zack Proser show how application-specific verification tools let coding agents detect incomplete work and repair it before asking for human attention. A wait-list app that displays success without saving anything anchors their case for deterministic checks, semantic judges, and durable evidence rather than confident completion messages.
key_points: Define done as an observable outcome and give the agent tools to verify it; successful builds, passing tests, and convincing prose can still conceal an unimplemented requirement.
Application-specific verifier CLIs turn manual developer checks—browser interaction, persistence inspection, network checks, and console review—into reusable agent feedback loops.
The Snack demonstration exposes a false success state: an email appears in the interface but disappears on reload because it was never persisted.
Use deterministic checks for concrete state and model-based judgments for semantic requirements, such as whether confirmation language overpromises what the system actually did.
Preserve receipts that identify the tested state, actions, results, and artifacts; a screenshot alone or evidence from an older code version is insufficient.
Specify outcomes and acceptance checks without overprescribing implementation steps, allowing agents to explore solutions while retaining a clear completion boundary.
Combine fast local repair loops with CI enforcement, preview verification, and rollout monitoring instead of treating any single verification layer as sufficient.
summary: Nisi and Proser argue that verification is both a safety requirement and the main constraint on scaling agent-assisted development. Their example is a Midnight Snack Club wait-list app: submitting an email updates the page and displays success, but refreshing removes it because nothing was persisted. A superficial UI check would approve broken behavior. The speakers therefore distinguish reviewing generated code from establishing that software delivers the intended result. Small tasks with explicit outcomes and available verification tools are easier to delegate than sprawling sessions repeatedly prompted to improve an unclear result.

Their application-specific Snack CLI packages the checks a developer would normally perform manually. It can start and stop the app, diagnose dependencies and session health, submit an email, reload, inspect storage and network activity, capture page snapshots and screenshots, and run proof commands. A deterministic proof can exercise a real user journey and verify resulting state, giving the agent specific failure feedback it can act on without waiting for a human. The intended loop is reproduce, observe, repair, and recheck. They emphasize that the implementation path need not be predetermined: agents can remain creative if the required destination and evidence of arrival are clear.

Two experimental tools illustrate broader orchestration patterns. Proser's CTX centralizes verification, checking external artifacts such as GitHub pull-request existence and merge status before satisfying workflow nodes. Nisi's Riker aims to manage the final stretch of a task, including review responses and subsequent checks, escalating only when needed. Both reflect the principle that completion status should derive from records rather than the worker's narrative. Receipts may include test results, screenshots, recordings, and references to checked artifacts. However, a screenshot is not sufficient proof if the application reached that state through an invalid path, and a passing receipt from an earlier source version cannot establish the current version's correctness.

The later exercises introduce semantic evaluation: persisting an email does not justify telling a user that a seat is confirmed when only wait-list membership was achieved. Fast model judges can assess that mismatch without exact-string coupling, while deterministic checks retain responsibility for concrete state. A randomized bug exercise also exposes problems in the workshop's own verification output, reinforcing the need to test verifiers. The speakers recommend preserving successful and failed runs as future evaluation data, enforcing checks through CI and appropriate hooks, and using previews plus production monitoring for deployments. In questions, they clarify that the principal benefit over existing CI tests is earlier autonomous correction with fewer human turns. Claims about very high PR throughput and self-evolving codebases remain anecdotal or forward-looking rather than demonstrated performance guarantees.
caveats: The supplied publisher transcript is untimed, and its metadata does not establish semantic completeness.
Snack is explicitly an application-specific teaching template, not a general-purpose verifier that can be adopted unchanged for arbitrary software.
Several live demonstrations fail or produce confusing output; the randomized bug exercise does not establish a clean end-to-end successful diagnosis.
Reported PR volumes, productivity improvements, and confidence in automated review are anecdotal and unsupported by controlled measurements in this source.
The discussion of self-evolving tooling describes anticipated workflows; the workshop does not demonstrate autonomous production safety.
action_items: Choose one important user journey and define observable completion criteria, including persistence after reload and the absence of misleading confirmation messages.
Wrap browser actions, state inspection, diagnostics, and proof checks in an application-specific CLI that agents can run repeatedly.
Return detailed, actionable errors so the agent can reproduce a failure, repair it, and rerun verification without another human prompt.
Attach receipts to each result, ensuring they correspond to the current code and include the actual interaction path rather than only a final screenshot.
Run the same checks locally and in CI, then extend verification to preview environments and monitor production rollouts for regressions.

videos.title: Evals for High-Stakes AI Agents — Doneyli De Jesus & Annabell Schäfer, Langfuse
videos.overview: Annabell Schäfer and Doneyli De Jesus demonstrate a continuous evaluation workflow for customer-facing agents in regulated industries. A fictional banking assistant connects tracing, privacy controls, expert annotation, mixed evaluators, deployment gates, and business dashboards into one improvement loop.
key_points: Traditional observability can report success while an agent fails semantically: an assistant may claim to issue a refund without ever calling the refund tool.
Reliable improvement connects tracing, monitoring, representative datasets, controlled experiments, and evaluation, with production failures feeding back into test cases.
High-stakes ground truth can come from domain-expert curation, shadow runs alongside manual processes, and human-reviewed workflows that gradually identify safe automation segments.
Expert annotation should be lightweight; free-text observations can be grouped into failure categories with an LLM and converted into explicit evaluation dimensions.
Combine deterministic checks with calibrated LLM judges rather than treating another model's judgment as inherently reliable.
Configuration changes can trigger dataset experiments in CI, with per-score thresholds producing an auditable pass/fail decision rather than an automatic guarantee of safety.
Automate instrumentation and repeated experiments while retaining human responsibility for task definition, dataset quality, hard limits, and evaluator calibration.
summary: The workshop begins with a distinction between infrastructure health and task success. A support agent can respond quickly, produce no errors, and receive a grateful reply while falsely claiming to have processed a refund. Detecting this requires visibility into actual tool execution, not merely the final message. Schäfer presents an AI engineering loop in which traces expose intermediate steps, monitoring identifies patterns worth investigating, datasets encode expected behavior, experiments vary system configurations, and evaluations measure the result. Internal, low-stakes tools may enter this loop through production tracing, whereas regulated customer-facing applications need stronger ground truth before broad deployment. Expert curation, shadow execution against manual work, and initially human-reviewed operation provide different routes to that foundation.

De Jesus demonstrates these ideas through a fictional banking assistant with customer personas, knowledge retrieval, tool calls, and risk scores. A masking function redacts sensitive card information before it is persisted in Langfuse, illustrating that observability must itself respect privacy requirements. Investment-advice requests are classified and redirected under the demonstration's banking policy. An audio example adds speech-to-text and inspection of the resulting interaction. The important object is the entire execution trace: inputs, model calls, available and invoked tools, outputs, and evaluation scores. Expected dataset outputs need not be exact answer strings; they can specify intent, required behavior, citations, or prohibited actions.

The proposed error-analysis process starts with humans inspecting a representative, filtered sample of traces. Domain experts receive simple annotation tasks and room for raw comments rather than being asked to design a taxonomy. An LLM then helps organize those comments into recurring failure categories, which become evaluation dimensions such as correctness, source inclusion, language matching, and appropriate register. Deterministic checks handle properties such as exact matches or regex conditions, while model judges assess less mechanically testable qualities. In the closing discussion, Schäfer recommends calibrating judges against human-labeled examples, ideally with multiple raters, and periodically checking that the calibration set remains representative.

Finally, versioned prompt changes trigger GitHub CI experiments against established datasets, with minimum thresholds for individual scores and retained evidence explaining the outcome. The demonstration does not automatically merge a passing change. Dashboards connect operational evidence to unresolved disputes, customer feedback, risk categories, and directional cost savings, allowing targeted investigation rather than indiscriminate trace review. The speakers reject both fully manual operation and vague requests for an agent to fix everything autonomously. Their preferred division of labor preserves human judgment over goals and standards while automating repeatable implementation work. They close with Langfuse learning resources and deployment questions, including ClickHouse storage, data export, and cloud or self-hosted operation.
caveats: The banking application and its data are explicitly fictional; dashboard figures illustrate a workflow rather than independently verified customer outcomes.
Restrictions such as refusing investment advice describe the demonstration's intended policy, not a universal legal rule for every financial assistant.
The supplied publisher transcript is untimed, and its semantic completeness is not independently proven.
action_items: Instrument tool execution and intermediate inputs and outputs, with sensitive-data masking applied before trace persistence.
Build a domain-expert-validated dataset covering normal requests, out-of-scope requests, and explicitly prohibited behavior.
Sample production traces for short expert reviews, cluster the comments into failure modes, and turn those modes into measurable checks.
Calibrate model judges against human labels and pair them with deterministic evaluators wherever the requirement permits.
Run configuration changes through CI evaluation thresholds and retain results for human release review; use production dashboards to select the next regression cases.

videos.title: Insurance Claims Are AI's Messiest Data Problem — Denys Linkov, Wisedocs
videos.overview: Denys Linkov explains why useful AI in complex medical claims starts with data cleaning and workflow transformation rather than a larger context window. He connects document-level extraction and calibrated evaluation to portfolio analytics, while keeping human decisions and claimant outcomes central.
key_points: Insurance AI inherits unfinished digitization: paper, fax, inconsistent electronic records, and jurisdiction-specific forms prevent simple enterprise-wide querying.
Complex claims combine medical disagreement, administrative handoffs, coverage questions, litigation, and organizational incentives; document extraction alone does not resolve these dependencies.
Duplicates, records belonging to other patients, poor scans, missing evidence, and enormous PDFs require dedicated preprocessing and detection systems.
Wisedocs uses a layered pipeline of OCR and images, extraction and classification models, human-verified summaries, and higher-level analysis rather than relying on a single general-purpose LLM.
The MLCR benchmark evaluates conciseness, accuracy, and completeness against expert-validated answers with calibrated judges; those dimensions can favor different models.
Reliable within-claim extraction enables cross-claim analysis of provider networks, travel, diagnosis patterns, treatment costs, and underwriting trends.
The speaker advocates auditable decision support with humans in the loop and acknowledges that organization-specific improvements do not establish industry-wide outcome gains.
summary: Linkov frames complex medical claims as a data and organizational problem whose ultimate goals should be better care, shorter delays, lower costs, and a better claimant experience. Enterprises are being asked to adopt AI before completing cloud migration, data integration, or even basic digitization. Insurance still receives paper, fax, PDFs, and differently configured electronic health records. Workers' compensation forms vary by state, while hospitals and doctors structure bills and notes differently. A seemingly straightforward question about which doctor achieves good outcomes therefore presupposes a consistent dataset that often does not exist. Governance, procurement, infrastructure access, and clear business objectives are prerequisites alongside model capability.

The focus is casualty insurance involving injuries, including auto liability and workers' compensation. Claims can span weeks or years because diagnosis, specialist review, utilization review, treatment, billing, coverage, and litigation create repeated handoffs. Conflicting incentives and slow processing can encourage repeated submissions or expose weak systems to fraud. At the data layer, duplicates may constitute a substantial share of incoming records, and documents from similarly named patients can become commingled. Linkov describes PDFs as large as eight gigabytes, missing X-ray reports referenced elsewhere, and contradictory medical assessments. These are not problems solved by simply uploading a short file to a chatbot; they require cleaning, cross-referencing, and explicit flags for reviewers handling many simultaneous cases.

Wisedocs' described architecture progressively concentrates information: OCR and image processing feed extraction models and classifiers, followed by human-verified summaries and additional analytical layers. Some tasks use specialized models rather than generative reasoning because cost, accuracy, and hallucination risk matter. To evaluate higher-level questions, the company developed MLCR with Artificial Analysis, spanning six question tiers and measuring conciseness, accuracy, and completeness against expert-validated answers with calibrated judges. Linkov reports rapid benchmark improvement and differing accuracy/completeness tradeoffs across providers, but emphasizes that downstream analysis is only useful if upstream extraction is trustworthy. Crucially, MLCR operates on clean data, so its results do not eliminate the real-world preprocessing burden.

Once individual claims become structured and reliable, organizations can analyze relationships among providers and lawyers, patient travel, co-occurring diagnoses, treatment pricing, and changes across lines of business. The intended payoff is better network decisions, fraud investigation, underwriting, and explainability—not simply faster summarization. Onboarding begins with representative files and agreement about business meanings, such as injury date versus report date, before expanding into a pilot and integrations. In questions, Linkov stresses auditable evidence and human decisions, while acknowledging that regulatory review remains context-dependent. He also distinguishes reported customer-specific savings from an industry-wide improvement in claim duration, which Wisedocs cannot yet claim.
caveats: The preserved duration is 2670 seconds from watch and publisher metadata; the videos-tab listing reports 2671 seconds.
Several charts and claim examples are illustrative or synthetic, and the transcript does not supply their full underlying data.
Benchmark improvement figures and provider comparisons are speaker-reported and lack enough model/version detail here for independent reproduction.
The speaker's estimate that human review removes many regulatory concerns is not a legal determination; the transcript provides no industry-wide proof of improved claimant outcomes.
The supplied publisher transcript is untimed, and its semantic completeness is not independently proven.
action_items: Audit incoming claims for duplicates, patient commingling, unreadable scans, missing referenced records, and unusually large files before adding advanced analysis.
Agree with business experts on field semantics and expected outputs using a small set of representative claims before starting a broader pilot.
Evaluate accuracy and completeness separately, using expert-validated answers and calibrated judges rather than one aggregate quality score.
Build verified document-level extraction before using its outputs for provider comparisons, pricing analysis, or portfolio decisions.
Keep decisions human-reviewed and source evidence auditable; measure claimant-facing outcomes separately from processing cost savings.

videos.title: Stop Telling Agents How
videos.overview: Dan Barrett, Raymond Weitekamp, and Jose Montes de Oca present OpenProse as a Markdown-based way to specify reusable agent workflows through composable outcome contracts. Demonstrations cover event-driven pull-request review and quant-model documentation, alongside candid discussion of model dependence, verification gaps, and the cost of leaving execution open-ended.
key_points: OpenProse emphasizes declarative outcome contracts: specify the required end state while allowing the underlying agent harness to choose execution details.
Programs and the runtime instructions are text, but they include a substantial type system and kernel rather than being ordinary informal Markdown prompts.
The framework delegates sub-agent mechanics to an existing harness, aiming to remain portable across approved models and local or hosted environments.
A standing job combines a contract with an event trigger, such as a webhook or schedule, rather than requiring a new chat conversation for every execution.
Independent review sessions assess work against contracts, creating feedback pressure without asking the original coding agent merely to approve its own output.
Successful traces can be codified into more procedural workflows, trading exploratory flexibility for lower execution cost and greater specificity.
Decision-model verification, semantic routing, dependency invalidation, and reinforcement learning are discussed as possible extensions, not established features of the demonstrated system.
summary: The presenters argue that communicating intent remains necessary even as models and harnesses improve. OpenProse moves that communication toward declarative, composable contracts describing required outcomes rather than prescribing every action. Borrowing from software engineering, they favor composition over inheritance and local specifications that can be combined into larger workflows. Raymond characterizes the system as text-based and event-driven: programs are Markdown, while recurring work begins from schedules or external events rather than chat. Users can ask an agent to draft a program and then inspect or edit it, avoiding the need to learn its syntax before gaining value.

The apparent simplicity hides substantial runtime instructions and a type system. A kernel teaches the coding agent how to interpret programs, while the existing harness supplies execution capabilities such as sub-agents and isolated contexts. Contracts can declare dependencies, tools, skills, inputs, outputs, and intermediate requirements; an unavailable required tool can be grounds not to run. The team positions this as an application layer above an organization's chosen harness and approved inference stack, including in-house deployments. They also qualify the declarative ideal: after an expensive model discovers a successful approach, its trace can be captured into more specific instructions to reduce future cost.

In the hosted demonstration, a voice request creates a standing pull-request review job framed as a skeptical senior developer. Spending-related actions require explicit confirmation. GitHub events trigger fresh review sessions that compare proposed changes with a contract, and development agents must incorporate the resulting feedback. Some examples required many review rounds. A second demonstration runs in Codex to generate documentation for a public SOFR-curve model, illustrating recurring financial-model governance work without exposing private bank data. The presenters report promising cost and quality results but acknowledge that auditor, compliance, and regulator acceptance remains a separate challenge requiring expert assessment.

The discussion makes several boundaries explicit. OpenProse suits repeated, reasonably well-understood workflows better than exploratory conversations in which the user does not yet know the desired result. Composed contracts can create intermediate checkpoints and express fan-out, review, and iterative patterns without fully fixing every execution step. However, output quality still depends on model and harness capability, and the agent can currently declare that it has fulfilled a contract. The team discusses independent decision models as potential cheap verifiers, routers, and detectors of stale dependencies, and discusses reinforcement learning over textual runs; these are future directions rather than demonstrated guarantees. Their central practical proposition is reusable operational knowledge expressed as inspectable, versionable text—not deterministic correctness merely because a workflow is written as a contract.
caveats: The preserved watch title is 'Stop Telling Agents How'; the publisher title is 'Stop Telling Agents How — Dan Barrett, Raymond Weitekamp & Jose Montes de Oca, OpenProse'.
The preserved duration is 2975 seconds from watch and publisher metadata; the videos-tab listing reports 2976 seconds.
The demonstrations and reported savings are presenter claims, without a reproducible external benchmark or completed regulatory acceptance evidence in the transcript.

The presenters explicitly acknowledge model-dependent behavior and agent self-declared completion; proposed decision-model verification and reinforcement learning were not demonstrated as implemented.
The supplied publisher transcript is untimed, and its semantic completeness is not independently proven.
action_items: Choose a recurring workflow with a known desired outcome, and write explicit acceptance conditions before automating it.
Separate mandatory tools, skills, and intermediate checkpoints from execution details the agent may choose for itself.
Use fresh review sessions against the same contract instead of relying only on the producing agent's self-review.
Capture a successful execution as a reusable workflow, then add procedural constraints where they demonstrably reduce cost or variability.
Test contracts against historical work and expert review, and require confirmation before enabling triggers that can incur ongoing spending.
